claim: KPMG estimates aggregate annual content spend by 12 leading US-based media/platform companies reached $210 billion in 2024, up from $142 billion in 2020, a 10% CAGR -- but this is a total industry investment figure with no creator-count denominator, so it cannot be converted into a per-creator average.
stance_target: Aggregate industry spend/payout figures without a creator-count denominator cannot be used to estimate average or median creator income
scope_conditions: 12 named companies (Comcast, Netflix, Disney, Amazon, YouTube, Paramount, Meta, Warner Bros Discovery, Spotify, Fox, Apple, Sony), primarily US-based; fieldwork April-August 2025; KPMG's own analysis of public filings and third-party data, not a creator survey
quoted_support: Annual content spend by top players now exceeds $200 billion, growing at a 10% compound annual growth rate (CAGR) since 2020... reaching an estimated $210B in 2024.
region: US-centric; 12 companies are 'primarily U.S.-based'; no Southeast Asia data

claim: KPMG's methodology attributes $32 billion in 2024 content spend to YouTube, but this figure bundles five distinct cost categories -- ad spend paid to creators, YouTube affiliate spend, YouTube Premium licensing costs, Channel Membership payouts, and NFL Sunday Ticket rights -- meaning it is not a pure creator-payout figure and includes licensing/sports-rights costs unrelated to individual creator income.
stance_target: The commonly cited $32B YouTube 'creator payout' figure should not be treated as money paid solely to individual creators
scope_conditions: YouTube, 2024, US-based analysis by KPMG using public filings and third-party reports; no recipient count given
quoted_support: YouTube 32 [billion]... Identified 5 areas of YouTube content spend using a combination of public filings and third-party reports: 1) Ad spend paid to content creators 2) YouTube affiliate spend 3) YouTube Premium licensing costs 4) Channel Membership payout to creators 5) NFL Sunday Ticket rights

claim: KPMG describes the platform monetization model (used by YouTube, TikTok, etc.) as having low barriers to entry but resulting in high competition among creators for revenue-sharing based on content performance, in contrast to the traditional studio model's high upfront investment but limited/curated access for new entrants.
stance_target: Structural description of why platform-based creator monetization is intensely competitive despite easy entry
scope_conditions: General industry analysis, not creator-level measurement
quoted_support: Low barriers of entry into the system, leading to the system being highly competitive... Revenue sharing from platform to content creators based on content performance

claim: Talent fees make up 20-30% of total production costs for large-budget productions, per KPMG's analysis, a cost structure cited as a reason AI is unlikely to rapidly displace overall content spend.
stance_target: Cost structure of high-budget content production (context for the platform/studio comparison, not creator-economy income directly)
quoted_support: For large-budget productions, talent fees still make up 20-30% of total production costs -- and an AI Tom Cruise is not the same as the real Tom Cruise.
